Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI systems have evolved from natural language tasks to using external tools to plan, retrieve, and act in technical domains. In smart grids, recent work applies agentic schemes to forecasting, optimization, and control, wrapping trusted solvers behind language interfaces and orchestrating multi-step workflows. The literature lacks a unified approach to designing and evaluating such systems. LLMs can produce numerically plausible yet physically infeasible outputs, evaluation protocols vary across tasks, and the boundary between what the model should and should not compute is implicit. This paper presents asolver-grounded designprinciple: a numerical result is reported only when it originates from a trusted tool and passes explicit verification. We review the building blocks of LLM and agentic AI systems for power systems: prompting strategies and agentic architectures. We instantiate the principle in four case studies: wind power forecasting, EV charging scheduling, power flow analysis, and contingency diagnosis, each comparing an LLM-only baseline against its solver-grounded counterpart on identical data and metrics. EV Agent reproduces the CVXPY optimum while reducing LLM-only unmet energy by 7.5–9.5×, and GridDebugAgent repairs 17/39 contingency cases while reducing total violations by 52.3%. We propose a four-group evaluation framework spanning task utility, solver-grounded correctness, faithfulness and safe failure, and cost and latency. A consistent division of labor emerges, the agentic system reliably orchestrates, retrieves, and explains, while
trusted tools compute and a verification gate decides what is reported. Keywords:Agentic AI, Large language models, Smart grids, Power systems
Introduction

Adoption of large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI systems has accelerated across research and industry. Google alone reported processing over 3.2 quadrillion tokens per month across its products in mid-2026, a sevenfold year-over-year increase [1], and Gartner projects that 40% of enterprise applications will embed task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5% a year earlier, with agentic AI accounting for an estimated $450 billion in enterprise-software revenue by 2035 [2]. These systems are now widely adopted for software engineering [3], scientific discovery [4], robotics [5], and domain-specific decision support [6]. Agentic systems combine LLMs with external tools, memory, retrieval, code execution, and trusted solvers so the LLM acts as planner and orchestrator rather than the sole source of answers [ 7, 8, 9, 10]. This shift from a single model call to a tool-use loop lets LLMs engage with multi-step engineering workflows where text alone is not enough. Agentic systems can decompose a problem, orchestrate solvers and data sources, inspect results, and revise plans, but these skills have barely reached engineering workflows that demand verified, physically grounded computation. Many power and energy systems tasks align closely with such an agentic workflow. Grid planning and operation, for example, combines language, data, physical models, optimization, and control in one procedure, where an operator ∗Corresponding authors. The data is heterogeneous, mixing textual artifacts such as grid codes, NERC reliability standards, outage reports, and vendor manuals with numerical streams from SCADA, weather forecasts, market signals, and asset records. The computational stack is also mixed, spanning forecasting models, power-flow and dynamic simulators, optimization solvers for economic dispatch (ED) and optimal power flow (OPF), and controllers for voltage and frequency regulation, each with its own interface and assumptions. The system must satisfy Kirchhoff’s laws, thermal and voltage limits, ramp rates, and security margins, and a violation carries operational, economic, or safety consequences. Renewable forecasting, distributed energy resource (DER) coordination, EV charging scheduling, grid planning, contingency analysis, and demand response all sit in this kind of workflow, where LLM reasoning and agentic systems can act as the layer that ties these components together. Power researchers have started to explore agentic AI’s promises in power industry. Current exploration falls into three major realms.Capability studiesevaluate LLMs on various domain-specific tasks, e.g., power flow analysis, OPF, EV scheduling, forecasting, and retrieval-based question answering over technical knowledge bases [ 11, 12]. Tool-augmented agentsplace trusted solvers behind a language interface. GridMind couples LLMs with OPF and

contingency solvers [13]. Grid-Agent pairs a planning agent with a sandboxed validation agent to remediate operatinglimit violations [14]. PowerGraph-LLM combines graph representations with in-context learning for OPF [15]. The PowerAgent roadmap integrates foundation models, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and agentic workflows [16]. LLM-based forecastinguses the LLM itself as the predictor, with promising results on wind power, load, and EV charging-station occupancy especially in data scarce settings [17, 18, 19]. All three lines share common failure modes. LLMs hallucinate, generating numerically plausible answers with no basis in underlying systems [20], and have no built-in mechanisms to enforce physical laws such as power flow equations, line thermal limits, or generator ramp rates. A fluent dispatch report can therefore describe a schedule violating these constraints without flagging it [ 11, 12]. LLM outputs are also hard to verify by inspection, since a correct numerical claim and an incorrect one are written with the same confidence and format, so an operator cannot judge credibility without re-running the trusted tool. This matters because grid outputs feed safety-critical control actions: a misreported voltage limit propagates into a dispatch decision, an under-delivered EV schedule becomes customer complaints and bill charges, and a missed contingency violation can damage equipment or cause blackouts. Power systems therefore need a deployment principle distinct from open-ended AI chatbots, one in which numerical

claims are produced by trusted tools and gated by explicit verification before they reach the operator. This paper takes this principle as its central thesis: LLMs and agentic AI systems for smart grids should be designed as a solver-grounded orchestration layer. The proposed design separates three roles: TheLLMinterprets the request, plans the task, calls tools, and generates the response. Thetrusted toolperforms the numerical computation. The verification gatechecks the result against physical and operational constraints before any value reaches the operator. Case studies in this paper span distinct smart grid task types, from forecasting and optimization to network analysis and diagnosis, and each is a setting where a plain LLM tends to produce plausible but infeasible numbers, so the solvergrounded design offers the clearest advantage. Related works

Literature on LLMs and agentic AI for smart grids have grown since 2023, and now spans four directions: (i) domain surveys, (ii) LLM-based forecasting and time-series modeling that use LLMs as prediction models, (iii) tool-augmented agents that wrap trusted solvers behind a language interface, and (iv) LLM-driven planning, optimization, and operations agents that embed LLMs in closed-loop workflows for grid operation and DERs. We review representative works in each and discuss how they motivate this tutorial.

Large Language Models and Next-Token Prediction

blocks.text: Large language models are probabilistic autoregressive sequence models, trained to predict the next token given previous tokens [49]. Formally, for a token sequencew 1:T , the model defines token probability as p(w1:T )= TY t=1 p(wt|w <t),(1) where T is the sequence length and w<t =( w1,...,w t−1) denotes the tokens preceding position t. The next-token-prediction objective in (1)–(2) has two implications for LLM-based smart grid systems. First, since generation is conditioned on the available context w<t, output quality depends strongly on the information provided at inference time. This motivates the prompting and context-construction methods discussed later, including structured, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting and RAG, which improve generation by supplying task descriptions, examples, reasoning structure, or external domain knowledge. Second, next-token prediction does not by itself enforce physical, operational, or numerical correctness. LLMs are trained to model patterns in large text corpora, not to guarantee physical laws such as Kirchhoff’s laws or optimization feasibility in power grids. The model also has no intrinsic way to distinguish quantities computed by a trusted solver from quantities inferred through language generation, and both appear equally fluent in the output. This explains why an LLM can produce a plausible but infeasible dispatch or an incorrect power flow result, and motivates the solver-grounded design rule of Section 2.3, where correctness is enforced with trusted tools and verification.
Frontier LLM Families and Training Procedures
heading_path: Frontier LLM Families and Training Procedures

blocks.text: Frontier LLMs split intoproprietaryfamilies accessed through managed APIs andopen-weightfamilies deployable locally, the latter suitable when operational data is not allowed to be accessed out of the utility’s network [50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56]. Across both, context length, multimodal-input support, and structured-output reliability vary by family and model size, and the model landscape evolves on a fast timescale of months. The frontier models share a common three-stage training pipeline: self-supervised pretraining on raw text, supervised fine-tuning on instruction-response data, and preference-based alignment. In thepretraining stage, the model learns broad statistical patterns of language by minimizing the next-token loss in (2) over a large unlabeled corpus. This gives general linguistic competence and world knowledge but targets no specific task or instruction format, so a pretrained-only model continues text fluently yet may not reliably follow instructions, answer in the expected format, or refuse unsafe requests. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)then adapts the pretrained model to instruction following using curated promptresponse demonstrations [57], updating the parameters by minimizing the token-level cross-entropy between predicted and target responses. SFT lets LLMs give structured, formatted answers and is a prerequisite for the tool calling, structured outputs, and conversational behavior agentic systems rely on. A final alignment stage optimizes the SFT model with human preference feedback so responses better match

The most common implementation isreinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where a reward model trained on human preference comparisons is used to optimize the LLM through reinforcement learning. blocks.text: The Solver-grounded Design Rule
heading_path: Frontier LLM Families and Training Procedures

blocks.text: The central design rule of this paper is that LLMs and agents should not be treated as sources of numerical truth in smart grid applications. Instead they act as interfaces, task planners, and orchestrators around trusted computational tools. These tools are central to safety-critical power systems practice, such as operating and planning studies already rely on power-flow solvers, OPF solvers, economic-dispatch optimizers, forecasting models, and simulators to enforce physical laws, operational limits, and feasibility. In current workflows, engineers configure cases, run these tools, inspect convergence and constraint violations, iterate across scenarios, and translate the outputs into operational reports. LLMs fit tool calling naturally because they can map natural language requests into structured tool inputs, select and sequence the right solver or data API, interpret logs and outputs, and explain results while leaving numerical computation to verified softwares. A numerical result should therefore be reported only if a trusted solver or simulator produces it and it passes explicit verification. This separates three roles. The LLM interprets the request, decomposes the task, selects tools, and explains results. The trusted tool performs the numerical computation. The verification gate checks whether the output is physically and operationally valid. Formally, let{Tk}K k=1 denote a set of trusted tools, such as power flow (PF) solvers, OPF solvers, ED optimizers, forecasting models, or domain-specific simulators. During an

Every reported numerical result must be traceable to trusted tool evidence in z, and the final response must satisfy all the verification conditions. When the task-level verification condition is not met, the system should explicitly report the failure mode rather than fabricate, extrapolate, or silently repair the answer. We refer to this behavior assafe failure. It adapts abstention from selective prediction [60] to the tool-use setting. This rule turns correctness from a property of the language model alone into a property of the overall LLM tool verification agentic system. A solver-grounded agentic system reports only numerical claims that are tool-derived, verifiable, and faithfully represented in the final response. One boundary deserves explicit statement. Atrusted toolhere does not mean an infallible source of truth. Instead, such a tool refers to a model, solver, or simulator whose assumptions are explicit and whose outputs can be checked for convergence, feasibility, and consistency with power-system constraints. This matches current practice: engineers rely on power-flow solvers, OPF solvers, scheduling optimizers, and contingency simulators, but still verify solver status, constraint residuals, voltage and line-flow limits, and input assumptions before using the results operationally. Such a principle applies most directly when such a tool exists for the reported quantity, as in the EV scheduling, power flow, and contingency case studies, where a solver computes the result and the verification gate checks its validity for the specified model and data. When no trusted solver exists, as in LLM-based wind power forecasting, the output cannot be solver-grounded in the same sense, and verification is limited to model- and output-level checks such as schema validity, range feasibility, consistency with historical data, and forecast-error evaluation against observations. This is the boundary of the solver-grounded regime rather than an exception: absent a trusted tool, the system should report predictions with their validation evidence and uncertainty, not as solver-verified quantities.

Where LLMs and Agents Add the Most Value

blocks.text: The solver-grounded rule of Section 2.3 guardrails what LLMs should not do in smart grid tasks. In practice, there are several recurring bottlenecks in solver-grounded smart grid workflows: data preparation, model specification, tool-run configuration, failure detection, scenario iteration, and technical reporting and interpretation. We do not propose these as a formal taxonomy but as a high-level synthesis of workflow patterns that motivate the observations and case studies in Section 6. First, bottlenecks live around rather than inside the solver.Data preparation, model setup, iteration, and reporting consume most expert time per scenario, while the solver call is fast. This supports positioning the LLM as an interface and orchestration layer rather than a numerical engine. The PFAgent case study (Section 6.3) shows the split: PandaPower’s Newton-Raphson solver computes the operating point, while the LLM parses multi-step queries, selects and sequences tools, tracks network state across turns, and synthesizes outputs into operator-readable responses. Second, iteration cost compounds with case complexity.As grid studies grow from one case to many scenarios, contingencies, assets, and operating conditions, the burden shifts from solving one well-posed problem to repeatedly specifying tasks, selecting tools, checking inputs, interpreting outputs, and revising the workflow. Here LLMs and agents add value as planners and orchestrators, since they decompose a request into subtasks, identify the required

blocks.text: data and tools, sequence tool calls, and adapt to intermediate results, leaving numerical computation to trusted solvers. The GridDebugAgent case study (Section 6.4) shows this by automating the diagnose-act-verify loop while preserving solver-grounded correctness. Third, verification itself is a bottleneck.The final output often combines numerical results, explanations, diagnostics, and recommendations. Even when the solver call is correct, the agent can misreport a value, omit a violation, or overstate a result’s validity. A solver-grounded design therefore separates three functions: i). the LLM interprets, plans, orchestrates, and explains, ii). trusted tools produce the numerical evidence, and iii). a verification gate decides whether the final answer is safe to communicate. Case studies quantify these roles, where EV Agent produces zero hard physical constraint violation across 20 benchmark days, whereas a standalone LLM baseline violates the 50 kW site cap.

We start with prompting-based systems, where the LLM produces the output directly from its input context, without external tool calls. We cover four strategies: structured, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting, and RAG. Fig. 6 compares them. Prompting is the simplest design layer and the baseline against which we compare the agentic systems of Section 4.

Structured prompting thus guides the model toward a well-organized response, while it could not self-guarantee numerical correctness. In smart grid applications, structured prompting helps replace an open-ended conversation with a controlled interaction. For an LLM summarizing an OPF or ED study, the role sets an operator persona, the context supplies the setup and physical constraints, the task requests the summary and any limit violations, and the output section fixes a table or JSON schema with prescribed fields and units. Such prompts have been used to specify economic-dispatch and unit-commitment problems for LLM-based solving [34, 32]. blocks.text: Few-shot prompting conditions the output on a few input-output demonstrations [ 49]. Each demonstration is a solved instance pairing an example input with its correct output, placed in the prompt just before the target query. blocks.text: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting asks the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer [64]. Because generation is sequential, the steps it writes become context for the final answer, so it decomposes a multi-step problem into sub-steps and builds the answer on its own reasoning. Making the steps explicit lets a reader follow how the answer was reached and improves quality on multi-step tasks. Fig. 4 illustrates CoT prompting on a power flow over-voltage diagnosis. In smart grid applications, CoT helps when the LLM explains solver outputs or supports human review. For a bus over-voltage, a CoT response can identify the violated limit, locate the affected bus, connect it to causes such as excessive local generation, and suggest actions such as adjusting inverter setpoints or transformer taps. Like the other techniques, CoT does not guarantee correct reasoning. It can produce plausible reasoning while making an arithmetic error or recommending an infeasible action, so the final response must still be checked against trusted computations and constraints. In power systems, CoT has been used within LLM assistants for dispatch operations [33]. blocks.text: RAG conditions the output on external documents retrieved at inference time [65]. An LLM answering from its internalized memory alone can produce plausible but outdated or unsupported statements. RAG addresses this in two stages. A retriever first searches an external knowledge source for the passages most relevant to the query. Those passages are inserted into the prompt as context, so the model answers from the retrieved evidence rather than its parameters alone, often citing the passages used. In practice, source documents are split into self-contained chunks, retrieved with metadata filters such as jurisdiction, voltage level, or effective date, and reranked for relevance. The prompt must return an explicit “insufficient evidence” response when the passages do not support an answer. Fig. 5 illustrates the pipeline on a grid-code compliance question. In smart grid applications, RAG helps because many task-relevant facts are not reliably stored in model parameters, including operating procedures, grid codes, market rules, reliability standards, tariffdocuments, and equipment manuals. Consider a question about whether a proposed operating action is allowed under a specific interconnection rule, market manual, or utility procedure. A RAG system first retrieves the relevant document sections, such as the applicable voltage range, effective date, or operating condition. The prompt then asks the model to summarize the rule, decide whether the action satisfies it, and cite the supporting passage. This matters most when the answer depends on local

blocks.text: Moving from prompting to agentic systems, the LLM is no longer restricted to its input context but orchestrates external tools, inspects intermediate results, and decides what to do next. We first define an agentic system and describe how it acts on the environment through API calls and tool use. We then cover five representative architectures: Reasoning and Acting (ReAct), plan-and-act, hierarchical, self-reflection, and multi-agent systems. We close with two cross-cutting components every architecture relies on: memory, which preserves state across steps, and the frameworks used to build agents in practice.

blocks.text: Agentic System Definition
heading_path: s requires the operator to curtail local generation.Source: Distribution Grid Code, Sec. 7.3.1, chunk #12

blocks.text: An agentic system extends the LLM beyond a single forward pass: instead of producing the answer directly from its input context, it solves a task through a sequence of reasoning steps and actions, where each action can query an external tool and return a new observation [7]. A common representation is the ReAct trajectory τt =(x,Thought 1,Action 1,Observation 1,...,Thought t,Action t,Observation t),(6) where x is the initial user input or task description andτt is the partial trajectory up to step t. At each step, Actiont∈A is drawn from an action space A that includes LLM reasoning steps, such as decomposing the task or drafting a candidate answer, and external tool invocations, such as calling a power flow solver, querying a database, or executing a script. The resulting Observationt∈O may come from an external tool, the operating environment, or the LLM’s own reasoning traces when intermediate thoughts and self-evaluations are fed back into later steps. The agent interleaves reasoning, action selection, tool interaction, and observation updates, and at each step decides whether to continue or terminate with a final answer or recommended action. This loop matches many smart grid tasks, where the system cannot answer from internal knowledge alone and must call a solver, retrieve external information, and check intermediate results before reporting. Consider N−1 contingency screening, where the agent is asked whether the system can survive the loss of a specified transmission line. It first

Practical agentic systems extend the basic reasoning–action–observation loop with memory, which preserves prior context, intermediate observations, and learned preferences across steps and sessions, keeping the agent from repeating work or losing information between solver calls. For safety-relevant tasks, a verification step is often added before the final answer to confirm that reported values match the trusted tool output and that recommended actions satisfy task-level constraints. The remaining subsections develop the loop’s components in turn: actions through API calls and tool use, common architectures, the role of memory, and the frameworks for building such systems.
Action: API Calls and Tool Use
heading_path: Action: API Calls and Tool Use

blocks.text: Tool use is central to solver-grounded smart grid workflows [7, 8]. The principle is that whenever a task requires real-time data, exact computation, or external documents, the agent should call a tool rather than infer the answer from text patterns. In power systems, such tools include data APIs, power flow simulators, optimization solvers, and verification routines. The LLM selects the tool, formulates its input, interprets the output, and reports the result faithfully, while the tool provides the evidence. A practical tool interface makes this contract explicit through input and output schemas, unit conventions, and failure messages, which reduce common errors such as loading the wrong case or reporting a wrong unit. It helps to distinguishread toolsfromwrite tools. Read tools retrieve or compute information without changing the environment, such as fetching weather forecasts, market prices, or event logs. Write tools modify it, for example by sending a control command, updating a schedule, or submitting a market bid. Because write tools create operational side effects, they should sit behind safeguards such as simulation, rule checking, approval workflows, or human-inthe-loop confirmation, which let agents support analysis, planning, and decision preparation while limiting unsafe or unauthorized actions. Tool use in smart grid agents is thus best understood as a task-specific grounding mechanism, not a generic capability: forecasting agents rely on data APIs and time-series models, scheduling agents on optimization

ReAct (Reasoning and Acting)interleaves reasoning with tool actions in a tight feedback loop [ 7]. At each step the agent produces a shortthought, executes anactionsuch as calling a tool, and reads back theobservation. The observation feeds the next thought, and the loop ends when the agent judges the task complete. Keeping thought, action, and observation separate makes the trace inspectable rather than one opaque output. ReAct fits workflows with a small action space and local decisions, such as iterative diagnosis or short corrective-action loops (e.g., GridDebugAgent, Section 6.4). Its limitation is the absence of a global plan. On long horizons the loop can drift or repeat steps, and reasoning at every step raises token cost. Plan-and-Actseparates planning from execution [ 66]. The agent first generates an explicitplan, a structured list of steps with declared inputs, outputs, and dependencies, then executes the steps in order. Reasoning is invoked again only on failure, such as a solver not converging, at which point the agent revises the remaining plan and resumes. The separation suits workflows with clear stage boundaries, where each stage has a different cost profile. In smart grids, planning studies such as data center siting or transmission expansion planning fit naturally. The agent plans the full sequence of stages, then executes each in turn, replanning only if a stage fails. Its limitation is that the run is only as good as the upfront plan. When the setting is hard to anticipate, an inaccurate plan forces repeated replanning.

Hierarchical agentsorganize decision making into levels [ 5, 67]. A higher-levelcontrollersets the goal and decomposes it into subtasks, while lower-levelworkerseach handle one subtask with their own tools. The controller aggregates worker outputs and decides whether to spawn more subtasks, revise the decomposition, or terminate. The pattern fits workflows that split into many independent subtasks whose results combine into one answer. In smart grids, N−1 contingency screening is a natural example. The controller dispatches one worker per outage to run the post-contingency power flow, aggregates the results into a ranked list of the most dangerous contingencies, and may spawn corrective-action workers for the critical cases. Its limitation is decomposition overhead. The controller must coordinate and merge worker outputs, and a poor decomposition degrades the answer. Self-reflection agentsinsert a self-critique step between the draft answer and the final output. After an initial response, the agent invokes itself as a critic, examines the draft for errors or constraint violations, and either accepts it or revises. Reflexion stores feedback across trajectories to guide future attempts [ 9]. Self-Refine critiques and refines the current output in place [68]. In smart grids, self-reflection adds an internal check for unsupported claims or inconsistencies between the answer and the tool evidence. This suits operator-facing reporting. Multi-agent systemspartition the workflow across specialized agents with defined roles and interfaces [ 10]. They are orchestration patterns, not models: each runs on an off-theshelf LLM through prompting and control flow, which is why the case studies in Section 6 use frontier models without fine-tuning. Memory Management

Memory lets an agent preserve state across steps: what has been tried, which tools were called, what observations returned, and whether outputs passed verification. It should be treated as a structured system component, not just a longer conversation history [9, 69, 70]. It includesshort-term memory, holding state within a single trajectory, and long-term memory, which carries across trajectories and holds episodic and semantic memories. Short-term memoryholds the working state within a single task: a scratchpad recording the current goal, steps taken, tool outputs received, and intermediate conclusions. Each reasoning step reads from it and writes back new information. Because it persists only for one trajectory, it is most exposed to context-window pressure: when the working state grows too large, items can be dropped or paraphrased, silently corrupting the reasoning [70]. In smart grid workflows, it keeps operational details such as the active network case and the latest solver output accessible across steps within a task. Long-term memorycarries state across tasks, typically as an external store [ 70], with two subtypes.Episodic memoryis the agent’s logbook of past runs, storing the task, tool calls, observations, failures, and the final verified 13

outcome of each [9].Semantic memorystores patterns and rules distilled from many runs: reusable guidance (“always verify solver status before reporting”), report templates, common causes of non-convergence, and standard corrective actions [69]. It gives consistency across tasks, but a faulty rule generalized from one episode propagates to every later run, so updates must be cautious. Verification status is an important filter: values from runs that failed verification should never be promoted to semantic memory as ground truth.
Frameworks and Tools for Building Agents
heading_path: Frameworks and Tools for Building Agents

blocks.text: Frameworks for agentic AI provide the engineering layer for defining agents, registering tools, managing memory, and deploying workflows. We group them by what they orchestrate, since the unit of orchestration most shapes how a smart grid workflow is built. Three classes differ in this unit: a single agent’s loop, a team of agents, or an explicit workflow graph, all relying on a connectivity layer of interoperability protocols. Because the ecosystem changes quickly, we describe each class by its durable engineering role and name representative tools only as illustrations. Agent SDKs and middleware orchestrate a single agent’s loop, with lightweight abstractions for tool use and logging (OpenAI Agents SDK [71], Semantic Kernel [72], Strands Agents [73]). They are the fastest to adopt but leave control flow implicit. Multi-agent frameworks orchestrate a team of agents, with abstractions for inter-agent messaging and role assignment (AutoGen [10], CrewAI [74]). They suit problems that decompose into distinct roles. Workflow orchestrators run an explicit graph of steps, with declared transitions, retries, and checkpoints (LangGraph [ 75], Microsoft Agent Framework [76]). They give the most control at the cost of more setup, and their explicit steps make a natural place to insert a verification gate. The three classes are not mutually exclusive. Interoperability protocols form the connectivity layer, standardizing agent-to-tool and agent-to-agent connections (MCP [77], A2A [78]). They orchestrate and verify nothing themselves but provide the substrate the framework classes use when external tools or
heading_path: Frameworks and Tools for Building Agents

blocks.text: remote agents enter the loop. In practice, power-system agents have favored lightweight custom orchestration over heavyweight frameworks. Most are bespoke single-agent loops with direct function calling, as in GridDebugAgent and PFAgent, or multiagent designs that separate planning from validation, as in GridMind [13] and Grid-Agent [14]. At the connectivity layer, MCP is emerging as the common substrate, adopted by X-GridAgent [27] and advocated in the PowerAgent roadmap [16]. Two patterns stand out. Framework choice is rarely standardized or reported across studies, which complicates reproducibility. Verification is seldom part of the framework layer, so it must be added explicitly. The unit of orchestration guides which framework class to choose: • Agent SDKsfor single-agent assistants, such as operator copilots, report generation, and the conversational PFAgent and GridDebugAgent of our case studies. • Multi-agent frameworkswhen the workflow decomposes into distinct roles, as in GridMind and Grid-Agent, which separate planning from validation. • Workflow orchestratorswhen a task has clear stage boundaries and steps must be verified before execution, such as multi-stage planning studies orN−1 contingency screening. • Interoperability protocolswhenever external tools or remote agents must connect, as in the MCP-based interface of X-GridAgent, independent of which framework orchestrates the task. In every case the framework supplies only the engineering layer: solver-grounded correctness still rests on the

blocks.text: Evaluation Protocol

Evaluation of LLM-based and agentic systems for smart grids must match the solver-grounded workflow of Section 2. A system that produces fluent but unverified numbers can score well on standard language metrics while still issuing physically infeasible decisions, and existing evaluation efforts were not designed for this setting. General agent benchmarks measure end-task success and tool-use competence but stay domain-agnostic and do not tie a tool’s output to physical feasibility [ 79]. RAG metrics assess faithfulness to retrieved text rather than to a trusted solver [80]. Selective-prediction criteria formalize abstention for classification rather than for verification-gated numerical reporting [ 60]. Recent surveys confirm that agent evaluation remains fragmented, and that agent-level hallucinations propagate across tool calls and reasoning steps in ways single-turn metrics miss [ 81, 82]. To our 14

knowledge, no existing framework couples these concerns into one protocol linking tool-output correctness to grid feasibility, the gap the protocol below addresses. We organize the evaluation around four metric groups that follow from the solver-grounded rule (Section 2.3). The rule reports a number only when a trusted tool computes it and verification passes. A numerical claim can therefore fail at three successive points on its path from computation to report. It can be inaccurate on the objective, infeasible at the tool boundary, or misreported in the final text. Producing a verified answer also consumes resources such as tokens, solver compute, and time. These four concerns define the groups. (i)Task utilityis accuracy on the primary modeling or optimization objective. (ii)Solver-grounded correctnessis whether the solution respects physical and operational constraints at the tool boundary. (iii)Faithfulness and safe failureis whether the natural-language report transmits the verified output without distortion and abstains when verification fails. (iv)Cost and latencyis the resources required to produce a verified answer. Each group exposes a failure mode invisible to the others. A low-error forecast can still violate a constraint, a feasible solver result can still be misreported, and a correct, faithful answer can still be too slow or costly to deploy. Groups (i) to (iii) exhaust the points at which a numerical claim can go wrong under the rule, while (iv) is the one concern orthogonal to correctness that gates deployment. Task utility alone, the metric most often reported in prior
capability studies [11, 12], hides exactly the constraint violations and report-level hallucinations that groups (ii) and (iii) expose.
Task utility

Task utility measures how good an answer is on the problem’s own terms, independent of how it was produced. It is the score we would assign if no LLM or agent were involved, reported identically for the LLM-only and solver-grounded variants so the two are directly comparable. For regression and forecasting tasks, we report a prediction-error metric against ground truth, such as mean absolute error (MAE), root-mean-square error (RMSE), or mean absolute percentage error. For classification and detection subtasks, we report an accuracy- or overlap-based metric such as F1 score. For constrained optimization, we report the achieved objective as an optimality gap relative to the optimal solver solution, paired with a task-completion metric such as the fraction of demand served. For diagnosis and remediation, we report a success metric such as repair rate with a partial-progress metric such as violation reduction. These families cover the most common smart grid tasks, and a task outside them adopts the native metric for its objective. Task utility is necessary but not sufficient. A standalone LLM can minimize MAE by interpolating recent history while still violating physical constraints, which is why the remaining three groups are needed. Some tasks are multi-objective, so a single scalar does not suffice. EV scheduling trades cost against unmet energy, and power flow reports voltage, flow, and balance errors. For these, task utility is a small vector of complementary metrics rather than one number.

Cost and latency capture the resources required to produce a verified answer, motivated by two concerns. First, the per-request footprint: at scale, each request consumes priced LLM tokens, tool and solver compute, and tool invocations, so a correct but expensive system may be impractical to run continuously. We implementGridDebugAgent, a solver-grounded ReAct agent [ 7] that iteratively diagnoses failures and executes remediation actions on electrical networks using the PandaPower library [87]. Strategy.GridDebugAgent has three components: (1) apreprocessing pipelinewith an evidence collector and rule engine that extracts network metrics and classifies failures, (2) aReAct agent coreusing GPT-4o (temp. 0.3, max 50 iterations) with OpenAI function calling, and (3) a tool suite covering five categories: query, simulation, diagnostic, grid actions, and memory management. GPT-4o is the backbone because the agent is built on OpenAI function calling, for which GPT-4o offered strong tool-use support when the system was built. The design is model-agnostic, and the PFAgent and EV Agent case studies exercise the same pattern across other frontier models. The grid-action tools include generation adjustment, load curtailment, line/shunt switching, and voltage control, while memory tools support network snapshots and conversation logging. Given a scenario, GridDebugAgent first applies diagnostic rules, then runs a diagnose→act→verify loop: it queries network state, proposes corrective actions (e.g., adjusting generator setpoints), executes them, re-runs power flow, and checks for remaining violations until the network is secure or max iterations are reached. blocks.text: Conclusion and Discussions

This tutorial paper presents an implementation-grounded tutorial on LLM-based and agentic systems for smart grids. Written for a power-systems audience, it reviews fundamental building blocks: prompting strategies and agentic architectures, with their memory, tool interfaces, and orchestration frameworks. On this foundation we propose the solver-grounded design rule, stating that a numerical result is reported only when it originates from a trusted tool and passes explicit verification. A four-group evaluation protocol spanning task utility, solver-grounded correctness, faithfulness and safe failure, and cost and latency is introduced. We instantiate both the rule and the protocol in four end-to-end case studies: wind power forecasting, EV charging scheduling, power flow analysis, and contingency diagnosis, each comparing an LLM-only baseline against its solver-grounded counterpart on identical data and metrics. A consistent pattern emerged. When the LLM is the interface and a trusted tool is the source of truth, the agent inherits the tool’s correctness. When the LLM is asked to compute, it does not. When no solver exists, as in forecasting, verification degrades from physical feasibility to output-level schema and range checks. Three limitations frame these findings. First, the case studies use off-the-shelf frontier LLMs without domain adaptation, so the comparisons measure prompting and architecture rather than fine-tuning. Second, they cover four representative tasks, not the full design space. Real-time control, market settlement, and protection coordination remain

open. Third, the protocol audits each system against its own solver-grounded counterpart rather than comparing two agents head-to-head. The most consequential future work follows from these gaps. Reusable verification libraries could expose per-unit, power-balance, and convergence checks behind a typed interface. Repair policies could turn the safe-failure path into a recoverable one without weakening verification. Verifiable-reward fine-tuning [59] could reuse verification-passed trajectories to train smaller tool-calling agents that run inside utility networks, keeping operational data on premises. None of these replace solvers. They reorganize the work around them by parsing the request, retrieving context, sequencing tool calls, and explaining a verified result. The operational impact of these systems, in our reading, will come not from new numerical capability but from compressing the engineering hours between a question an operator asks in natural language and an answer a control system can act on.

Failure Analysis Across Case Studies

Table S2 documents the scenarios where each system reaches its limit. EV Agent and PFAgent preserve the solver result on every evaluated case, so their hard failures are confined to the LLM-only baselines. GridDebugAgent is where the agentic framework itself leaves scenarios unsolved, and wind forecasting has no solver, so its failures are prompting-level. Every failure above is measured, not narrated. The shared checker recomputes each metric on the system the agent produced, so partial repairs and residual violations surface in the reported numbers rather than being masked. This is the safe-failure behavior of Section 2.3 in practice: the system reports the shortfall instead of fabricating a fix.
